title: The women of Saidpur
hookLine: a wedding photo in a ruined house: Guru Nanak's lament on ang 417 remembers the women as brides before it mourns what was done to them

lines: A WEDDING PHOTO ON A BROKEN WALL.
cards: After a war, reporters walk through broken houses, and sometimes the camera stops on one thing left on a wall: a wedding photo. A bride in red, a groom beside her, everybody smiling. It says more than a casualty count.
These were people with a before. In Raga Asa, Guru Nanak sings a lament for the women caught in the invasion. Tradition ties it to Saidpur, the town of Bhai Lalo.
And before the hymn mourns, it does something unexpected. It remembers their weddings.

teach.b: First, the before. In paraphrase, the hymn says: those heads that were lovely with braids, the parting of the hair filled with vermilion. When they were married, their husbands looked handsome beside them.
They came in palanquins decorated with ivory. Water was waved over their heads, and fans glittered beside them. Guru Nanak takes time over this.
He lets us see them as brides, honored and celebrated. Second, the after. The same heads, the hymn says, are now shorn, and dust is in their throats.
They lived in palaces, and now they're not allowed even to sit near.

teach.h: THE AFTER: DUST AND BROKEN PEARLS.
teach.b: Strings of pearls are broken, and ropes are put around their necks. He doesn't go further into what was done. He doesn't need to.
The before makes the after unbearable. Third, why tell it this way.
A lament that only counted the dead would make them a number.
This one makes them people, with their wedding day kept right beside their suffering. It's a way of mourning that refuses to let war shrink anyone. Fourth, who is speaking.
Guru Nanak, a man, singing about women whose suffering could easily have been folded into someone else's story. He doesn't fold it in.
He gives them stanzas of their own, set in scripture, where they are still sung and read. Not a footnote to the invasion, but people the Guru mourned with their before remembered.

how: This ashtpadi of Guru Nanak in Raga Asa is sung in kirtan as part of Gurbani, and some Sikhs recall it when remembering those who suffered in war and partition.

games.q: what does “the women of saidpur” mean?
o: the brides at Bhai Lalo's family wedding
women the hymn mourns, remembered first as brides
warrior women who fought off the invaders

games.q: the lament on ang 417 — tap the pairs.

s: the lament only describes the attack
it first remembers the women as brides: palanquins, ivory, water waved over their heads.
tradition ties this hymn to Saidpur, the town of Bhai Lalo
the hymn itself doesn't name the town; tradition links it.

games.q: you're singing a lament for women hurt in an invasion. where do you begin?
o: with the generals who led it.
games.why: Guru Nanak begins with the before: braids and vermilion, handsome husbands, palanquins of ivory. then the after.

practice: Bring to mind women living through war or its aftermath, anywhere, in any time, and give each one a before, a kitchen, a classroom, a wedding, a job she was good at, so she isn't seen only in the worst moment.
If you pray, hold them before God in your tradition's way or say Waheguru on each out-breath; if not, simply keep them company in your thoughts.
If this story touches harm done to you or someone close, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The women of Saidpur. Guru Nanak's lament on ang four seventeen, which remembers the women as brides, and mourns what the invasion did to them. Today's word.

orig.note: sandhoor: vermilion, worn in the parting of the hair; the hymn's picture of the women as brides.

carryVoice: Your line: he mourned them. Their before belongs in the story too. Until tomorrow, friend.

sources.ref: Asa, Mahala 1, ashtpadi ('jin sir sohan pattee-aa maangee paae sandhoor'), Ang 417
